We continue to assume that the input is a number greater than zero. As you learned in Week 1, input() returns a string, so float() converts that string to a number and allows a weight such as 1.5. The decision diamond has become the condition weight <= 2, and the two assignments correspond to its paths. The final display statement follows both paths. A weight of 1.5 or 2 produces the lower rate, while a weight of 3 produces the higher rate.

You also met comparison operators in Week 1. A comparison produces True or False; here, that result can determine which path the program follows.

An expression that produces True or False is a Boolean expression. Here, weight <= 2 determines which path runs. Remember that = assigns a value, while == compares values for equality.

10.2 The if Statement and Indentation

An if statement runs one or more statements when its condition is True. Consider a program that displays a message for packages in the lower weight range:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    print("The lower shipping rate applies.")

print("Thank you for checking our shipping rates.")

For a weight of 1.5, both messages appear. For a weight of 3, the first message is skipped, but the thank-you message still appears.

In Python, the statements controlled by an if form a block. Indentation shows which statements belong to that block. The if header ends with a colon, and every statement in its block is indented beneath it at the same level. Use four spaces for each indentation level.

Returning to the previous indentation level ends the block. A statement at that level is outside the if block. Moving a statement into the block therefore changes when it runs:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    print("The lower shipping rate applies.")
    print("Thank you for checking our shipping rates.")

Now both messages belong to the if block. For a weight of 3, neither appears. Both versions are valid Python, but their indentation gives them different behaviour.

An if statement on its own either runs its block or skips it. Adding else gives the program an alternative block, as in our shipping calculator:

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

Exactly one assignment runs. The else has no condition of its own: it covers every case rejected by the if condition. Its header ends with a colon and aligns with the if to which it belongs.

The display statement belongs after the entire selection because both paths need it. This combines selection with the surrounding sequence of input, processing, and output.

10.3 Choosing Among Several Paths

Now consider a fictional cinema with three ticket prices:

Age Ticket Price
Younger than 13 Child $8
13 through 64 Adult $14
65 or older Senior $10

The customer enters an age, and the program displays the corresponding price. For now, we assume the input is a whole number greater than or equal to zero. We will handle negative ages later in this chapter.

One condition separates two paths. To choose among three prices, we need another condition. The keyword elif means “else if.” Python checks its condition only when the earlier conditions in the same chain were False:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

if age < 13:
    ticket_price = 8
elif age >= 65:
    ticket_price = 10
else:
    ticket_price = 14

print("Ticket price: $", ticket_price, sep="")

Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first matching branch, one of the chain’s alternative paths. For an age of 70, age < 13 is False and age >= 65 is True, so Python assigns the senior price. For an age of 10, the first condition is True, so Python does not check the elif. For an age of 30, both conditions are False, so the else block assigns the adult price.

An if-elif-else chain can contain several elif clauses. The final else is optional, but when present it must come last. Without an else, no branch runs when every condition is False. In this program, the earlier conditions leave ages 13 through 64 for else. The shared display statement then runs after the chain.

Condition order matters when conditions overlap. Consider this incorrect attempt:

if age >= 13:
    ticket_price = 14
elif age >= 65:
    ticket_price = 10
else:
    ticket_price = 8

An age of 70 satisfies age >= 13, so the first branch assigns the adult price. Python never reaches the senior condition. Arrange overlapping conditions so that an earlier branch does not capture a case intended for a later one.

10.4 Combining Conditions

In Week 1, you previewed the Boolean operators and, or, and not: and requires both conditions to be True, or requires at least one of them, and not reverses its condition. We can now use them to combine comparisons in a single condition. We will study Boolean logic in more depth later in the course.

For example, an adult ticket applies when the age is at least 13 and at most 64:

if age >= 13 and age <= 64:
    print("The adult ticket price applies.")

Both comparisons must be True. An age of 30 satisfies both, while an age of 70 fails the second.

For a non-negative age, either the child condition or the senior condition identifies a customer who does not pay the adult price:

if age < 13 or age >= 65:
    print("A child or senior ticket price applies.")

The result is True when either comparison is True. In this example, that means the age is in the child or senior range.

A common mistake is to leave out part of a comparison. To check whether an age is exactly 12 or exactly 65, write each comparison in full:

age == 12 or age == 65

Do not write:

age == 12 or 65

The second expression does not compare age with 65. As a condition, it succeeds for every age; we will see why later in the course.

10.5 Independent and Nested Decisions

An if-elif chain chooses at most one branch. Separate if statements make independent decisions, so more than one block can run.

Suppose the cinema displays one message for a child ticket and another for a booking of five or more tickets:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
ticket_count = int(input("How many tickets are you buying? "))

if age < 13:
    print("A child ticket is needed for this customer.")

if ticket_count >= 5:
    print("Please collect this booking at the group counter.")

For an age of 10 and a ticket count of 5, both messages appear. Changing the second if to elif would make Python skip the ticket-count check whenever the child condition was True. Use separate if statements when both actions may occur. Use an elif chain when the branches are alternatives.

A nested decision places one decision inside another decision’s block. This is useful when the inner decision should happen only on a particular outer path.

We can use nesting to check whether an age is valid before choosing a ticket price. The first decision separates invalid ages from valid ones. Ticket selection happens only on the valid path, so it is nested inside that path. Here is that design expressed in Python:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

if age < 0:
    print("Age must be zero or greater.")
else:
    if age < 13:
        ticket_price = 8
    elif age >= 65:
        ticket_price = 10
    else:
        ticket_price = 14

    print("Ticket price: $", ticket_price, sep="")

The outer decision checks whether the age is negative. If it is, the program displays an error; otherwise, the inner selection chooses the ticket price. Its headers are indented four spaces, and their blocks are indented eight spaces. The final print() returns to four spaces, so it follows the inner selection but remains inside the outer else. A negative age therefore never reaches the price display.

This program checks one input and then ends. Asking again after an error will require a loop; Chapter 9 represented that repetition with a loop-back arrow. The program also assumes that int() can convert the input. We will handle failed conversions separately.

10.6 Testing Decision Paths

Testing compares what a program does with what it should do. Debugging finds and fixes the cause when those results differ.

In Chapter 9, we checked a design by following a path through its flowchart. Now we can run the Python program with chosen inputs and compare the displayed results with the cinema’s rules.

For the version that checks negative ages, useful cases are:

Age Expected output Why this case helps
-1 Age must be zero or greater. Just below the accepted range
0 Ticket price: $8 Lowest accepted age
12 Ticket price: $8 Last age in the child range
13 Ticket price: $14 First age in the adult range
64 Ticket price: $14 Last age in the adult range
65 Ticket price: $10 First age in the senior range

These boundary cases sit at or beside the points where behaviour changes. They help expose mistakes such as using <= where < was intended.

Ordinary values such as 10, 30, and 70 are also useful because they exercise each price branch. Passing these tests provides evidence that the program follows the requirements, although a finite set of tests cannot cover every possible input.

Choose the expected result from the requirements before running the program. Otherwise, it is easy to accept the program’s answer simply because it produced one.

When a result differs from what you expected, trace that input through the code. Check:

  • The conditions: do the comparisons include the correct boundaries?
  • The branch order: does an earlier condition capture the input unexpectedly?
  • The indentation: does each statement belong to the intended path?

For independent decisions, include cases where both conditions are True, only one is True, and neither is True. This can reveal an accidental change from two if statements to an if-elif chain.

10.7 Summary

Selection chooses which statements run for a given input. An if statement can run or skip a block, else provides an alternative, and elif extends the choice to more paths. Indentation defines the blocks, and a chain runs only its first matching branch.

Boolean operators combine conditions. Separate decisions allow multiple actions, while nesting makes one decision depend on another. Test each path and the values where behaviour changes, using the requirements to determine the expected results.

10.8 References and Further Reading

  • Python Tutorial: if Statements: examples of if, elif, and else.
  • Python Language Reference: The if Statement: the formal structure and execution rules for selection.
  • PEP 8: Style Guide for Python Code: conventions for indentation and naming.
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 6: flow control, Boolean expressions, and the if statement.

11 Working with Strings

So far, we have used strings mainly to read input and display messages. Working more closely with text requires us to look inside those values. A string is an ordered sequence of characters: we can find its length, select a character by its position, and examine the text it contains.

We can also combine strings, adjust capitalization, remove surrounding spaces, and insert calculated values into messages. These operations produce new values without changing the original string. Understanding that distinction will help us use strings correctly as our programs become more involved.

11.1 Strings and String Literals

Chapter 6 introduced string literals, and Chapter 7 introduced str as the type used for strings. We can now distinguish the notation written in code from the value it produces.

A string literal is the quoted notation used to write a string value directly in source code. The surrounding quotes mark the literal’s boundaries; they are not part of the value.

>>> "COMP 1510"
'COMP 1510'
>>> 'hello'
'hello'
Closer Look

The REPL uses quotes to show that a result is a string, and may choose a different quote style from your literal. print() displays the string’s contents without those surrounding quotes, so the same value can look different in the two displays.

You can use single or double quotes. Choosing the outer quotes lets you include the other kind inside the text:

print("It's easy")
print('She said "hi"')

The empty string, written "", contains no characters. It is still a string, just as zero is still a number.

11.2 Escape Sequences

Some characters affect how text is displayed. A newline moves text to the next line, and a tab adds horizontal spacing. Python writes these characters inside a literal with an escape sequence: a backslash followed by a character with a special meaning. For example, \n represents one newline character.

Escape sequence Meaning
\n Newline: moves output to the next line
\t Tab
\\ A single backslash
\' A single quote
\" A double quote 
print("Line one\nLine two")
print("Name:\tAda")

The first statement displays its text on two lines. The second inserts a tab between Name: and Ada. Although \n is written with two characters in the source code, it represents one newline character in the string.

Often, choosing the other quote style is easier than using an escape. For example, the apostrophe in "It's easy" does not need to be escaped because the string literal uses double quotes.

11.3 Characters, Length, and Indexes

Each letter, digit, space, or punctuation mark in a string counts as one character. The built-in len() function returns the number of characters.

Each character sits at a numbered position called an index. Python numbers indexes from zero:

The string "Python" contains six characters, with indexes from 0 through 5. In a non-empty string, the first index is 0 and the final non-negative index is one less than the length.

Square brackets after a string select the character at an index:

>>> word = "Python"
>>> len(word)
6
>>> word[0]
'P'
>>> word[1]
'y'
>>> word[len(word) - 1]
'n'

Asking for an index outside the string raises an IndexError. The valid indexes of this six-character string run from 0 to 5, so word[6] fails.

The expression len(word) - 1 calculates the final index without assuming a particular string length. When text comes from input, we must first check that it contains at least one character:

name = input("Name: ")

if len(name) > 0:
    print("The first character is", name[0])
    print("The final character is", name[len(name) - 1])
else:
    print("No name was entered.")

The condition protects both indexing expressions. An empty string has length 0 and has no valid indexes, so trying name[0] without checking would raise an IndexError.

Negative indexes count from the end of a string. The index -1 refers to the final character:

>>> word[-1]
'n'

Python can also extract several characters at once. We will study that operation, called slicing, alongside lists later in the course.

11.4 Strings Are Immutable

Selecting a character does not mean that you can replace it. This assignment fails:

>>> word[0] = "J"

Python raises a TypeError. Strings are immutable, which means that an existing string value cannot be changed in place.

If a string cannot be changed in place, how can a program produce different text? A method is a function that belongs to a value, and strings provide many of them. Some methods return a new string while leaving the original unchanged.

You have already seen calls such as len(course), where the value goes inside the parentheses. A method call uses a different form: course.upper(). Here, course refers to a string, the dot connects it to the method named upper, and the parentheses call that method. The call returns an uppercase version of the string, which you can assign to a name:

course = "Introduction to Programming"
uppercase_course = course.upper()

print(course)            # Introduction to Programming
print(uppercase_course)  # INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING

You can also assign the result back to the same name:

course = course.upper()

This does not change the original string. It makes course refer to the new string.

This difference explains a common surprise:

>>> name = "Ada"
>>> name.upper()
'ADA'
>>> name
'Ada'

The method produces a result, but this example does not store it. If the program needs the uppercase value later, it must assign the result to a name:

>>> uppercase_name = name.upper()
>>> uppercase_name
'ADA'

The same principle applies throughout this chapter: an operation can inspect a string or produce another value, but it does not edit the original string.

11.5 Combining Strings

Joining strings is concatenation. Python uses the + operator for it:

>>> first = "COMP"
>>> course = first + " 1510"
>>> course
'COMP 1510'

The * operator repeats a string a whole number of times:

>>> "ha" * 3
'hahaha'

The + operator cannot directly combine a string and a number. Although str() can convert a number first, f-strings are usually a clearer way to mix text with values.

11.6 A Few Useful String Methods

We have already used upper() to produce uppercase text. Here are six useful string methods. In the table, s is the string being used and t is the text to search for:

Method Result
s.upper() A new string with each letter uppercase
s.lower() A new string with each letter lowercase
s.isupper() True if the string has at least one letter and all its letters are uppercase
s.islower() True if the string has at least one letter and all its letters are lowercase
s.strip() A new string with surrounding whitespace removed
s.find(t) The index of the first occurrence of t, or -1 if it is absent 
>>> course = "  Comp 1510  "
>>> course.strip()
'Comp 1510'
>>> course.lower()
'  comp 1510  '
>>> "COMP 1510".isupper()
True
>>> "comp 1510".islower()
True
>>> "Comp 1510".islower()
False
>>> "COMP 1510".find("M")
2
>>> "COMP 1510".find("z")
-1

These methods leave the original string unchanged, but their results have different types. upper(), lower(), and strip() return strings; isupper() and islower() return True or False; find() returns an integer position, or -1 when the text is absent. That -1 reports a failed search; it does not mean that a match was found at the final character.

strip() removes whitespace from the beginning and end, including spaces and tabs. It leaves spaces inside the text intact, so " Comp 1510 ".strip() preserves the space between Comp and 1510.

What a method returns determines how you can use it. A method that returns a string can provide cleaned or normalized text:

name = input("Name: ")
name = name.strip()
print("Hello,", name)

Methods are also useful in conditions. Converting text to lowercase before comparing it lets the program accept several capitalizations:

answer = input("Continue? ")
answer = answer.strip()
answer = answer.lower()

if answer == "yes":
    print("Continuing")
else:
    print("Stopping")

First, strip() removes surrounding whitespace. Then lower() produces lowercase text, allowing "yes", "YES", and " Yes " to satisfy the same condition. Each assignment makes answer refer to the next result.

Python provides many more string methods. You do not need to memorize a large list. Learn a small useful set now, and consult the string methods documentation when a program needs something else.

11.7 Formatting Output with F-Strings

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f. Expressions inside braces are evaluated and placed into the text:

>>> name = "Ada"
>>> age = 19
>>> f"{name} is {age} years old"
'Ada is 19 years old'
>>> f"Age next year: {age + 1}"
'Age next year: 20'

The braces can contain a variable or another expression that produces a value.

Compare two ways to display the same result:

name = "Ada"
score = 92

print(name, "scored", score)
print(f"{name} scored {score}")

Both statements work. The f-string keeps the spaces and wording together, making the intended output easier to see in the program.

A colon after an expression introduces a format specification. Writing :.2f displays a number with exactly two digits after the decimal point, rounding the displayed value when needed:

>>> shipping_rate = 8
>>> f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}"
'Shipping rate: $8.00'

Formatting changes the text produced for display; it does not change the value stored in the variable.

Here is the shipping calculator from Chapter 10 with its output formatted using f-strings. As before, this version assumes the user enters a positive numeric weight:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

print("COMP Couriers")
print(f"Weight: {weight} kg")
print(f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}")

Use f-strings when output combines text with values. They keep the output pattern readable and give you control over how numbers appear.

F-strings create strings; they do not print by themselves. In the REPL, Python displays the resulting value, but a program normally passes the f-string to print() or assigns it to a name:

customer = "Ada"
message = f"Welcome, {customer}!"
print(message)

This prints Welcome, Ada!. Building a string and displaying it are separate operations, even when a program performs them in the same statement.

11.8 Summary

A string is an immutable sequence of characters. A string literal is text written directly in source code to create a string value. len() returns the number of characters, and an index selects one character from the sequence.

Strings cannot be changed in place, but expressions and methods can produce new strings. The methods upper(), lower(), and strip() return new strings, while find() returns an integer index. An f-string places the values of expressions into text, and :.2f displays a number with two digits after the decimal point.

11.9 References and Further Reading

  • String methods: the complete list of methods supported by strings.
  • F-strings in the language reference: the formal syntax of formatted string literals.
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 7: strings, immutability, and f-string formatting.

12 Using Python Modules

Python programs often use code that is already available. You have called built-in functions such as input() to read text, int() to convert a value, and print() to display it. Python also includes a standard library of reusable tools.

A module groups related functions and values. To use functions from a module such as math, you first import it. We will use math and random to see how to access their tools and use the results in calculations.

12.1 Importing a Module

The import statement makes a module available under its name. Imports normally appear at the top of the file, before the statements that use them. This example uses math.sqrt() to calculate a square root:

import math

number = float(input("Enter a non-negative number: "))
root = math.sqrt(number)
print(f"Square root: {root:.2f}")

The expression math.sqrt(number) uses dot notation: math identifies the module, sqrt selects its square-root function, and the parentheses call that function with number.

The example assumes that the user enters a number greater than or equal to zero. The prompt describes the expected input; it does not check it. We will add input checks when we study loops.

The dot also appeared with string methods in Chapter 11. The name before the dot tells you where the operation comes from:

  • name.upper() calls a method on the string referred to by name.
  • math.sqrt(25) calls a function provided by the imported math module.

After import math, write math.sqrt(25); the import does not create a separate name called sqrt.

12.2 The math Module

The math module contains mathematical functions and constants. We will use two of them here:

Name Purpose Example
math.sqrt(x) Returns the square root of x math.sqrt(25) produces 5.0
math.pi Python’s floating-point approximation of π\piπ Approximately 3.141592653589793

math.pi is a value, so it is used without parentheses. math.sqrt is a function, so parentheses call it:

>>> import math
>>> math.pi
3.141592653589793
>>> math.sqrt(81)
9.0

12.2.1 Calculating the Area of a Circle

For a circle with radius rrr, the area is A=πr2A = \pi r^2A=πr2. This program uses math.pi for π\piπ and assumes the user enters a positive numeric radius:

import math

radius = float(input("Enter the circle radius: "))
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
print(f"Area: {area:.2f}")

Python squares radius with ** 2 and multiplies the result by math.pi. The f-string displays two decimal places without changing the value stored in area.

12.2.2 Calculating Distance with math.sqrt()

Suppose two points are 3 units apart horizontally and 4 units apart vertically. By the Pythagorean theorem, the distance between them is 32+42=5\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 532+42​=5. The program first stores the sum of the squares in squared_distance, then passes that value to math.sqrt():

import math

horizontal = 3
vertical = 4
squared_distance = horizontal ** 2 + vertical ** 2
distance = math.sqrt(squared_distance)

print(f"Distance: {distance:.2f}")

horizontal and vertical are starting values. squared_distance is an intermediate variable holding 25. math.sqrt() returns 5.0, which is assigned to distance and displayed. You could pass the sum directly as math.sqrt(horizontal ** 2 + vertical ** 2); the name lets you inspect it.

12.3 The random Module

The random module provides randint(a, b) for choosing an integer between two limits:

>>> import random
>>> random.randint(1, 6)
4
>>> random.randint(1, 6)
1
Reading The Output

The numbers above are sample results, not output your calls must match. A repeated roll can return the same number; that alone does not mean the program is stuck.

Both limits are included, so random.randint(1, 6) can return any integer from 1 through 6, like a six-sided die. The limits must be integers, and the first must not exceed the second.

12.3.1 Choosing a Random Point

A program can import more than one module. This example chooses a point at random and calculates its distance from the origin:

import math
import random

x = random.randint(-5, 5)
y = random.randint(-5, 5)
distance = math.sqrt(x ** 2 + y ** 2)

print(f"Point: ({x}, {y})")
print(f"Distance from the origin: {distance:.2f}")

The names before the dots identify which module supplies each function. Two calls to random.randint() choose the point’s x and y coordinates; math.sqrt() uses them to calculate the distance. A later run may choose a different point, or the same one again.

When you need more from a module, check its documentation for available functions, the arguments they take, and the values they return.

12.4 Summary

The standard library is ready-made code that comes with Python. An import statement makes a module available, and dot notation selects a function or value from that module.

The math module provides math.sqrt() and the value math.pi. The random module provides random.randint(a, b), which returns a whole number from the inclusive range a through b. Keeping the module name visible makes the source of each library tool clear.

12.5 References and Further Reading

  • The Python Standard Library: the official index of modules that ship with Python.
  • math: Mathematical functions
  • random: Generate pseudo-random numbers
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 12: importing and using modules.

13 Repetition in Python

A program often needs to perform the same work more than once. It might ask again after invalid input, examine each character in a string, or keep a running total. Writing a separate statement for every repetition becomes impractical when the input determines how many are needed.

A loop lets us write the repeated steps once and control how often they run. Chapter 9 showed this idea with a loop-back arrow in a flowchart. We will now express it in Python using while and for.

13.1 From Repeated Statements to Loops

Suppose a program needs to display the numbers from one through five. One approach is to write five separate statements:

print(1)
print(2)
print(3)
print(4)
print(5)

This works, but the program describes every repetition separately. Extending it to one hundred would require ninety-five more statements. If the counting rule changed, many lines might need to change with it.

The repeated lines can be replaced by a rule: display the current number, increase it, and stop after five. One pass through a loop’s block is an iteration.

Before writing a loop, answer three questions:

  1. What values, if any, must be set before the repetition begins?
  2. Which statements need to run during each iteration?
  3. What will change from one iteration to the next, and how will the loop know when to stop?

Python provides two loop statements. A while loop repeats as long as a Boolean condition is True. A for loop takes items from a sequence one at a time; in this chapter, the sequence will be a string. We will begin with while because its condition makes the decision to repeat or stop explicit.

13.2 The while Statement

The while loop repeats its block while its condition is True. This loop counts from one to five:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

Three parts make this loop work:

  1. Before the loop, count is initialized to 1.
  2. At the top of every pass, Python tests count <= 5. If it is True, the indented block runs. If it is False, the loop ends.
  3. The statement count += 1 increases count by one before the next condition check.

A trace of the iterations shows how the values change and why the loop stops:

Condition check count at the test count <= 5 Body prints
1 1 True 1
2 2 True 2
3 3 True 3
4 4 True 4
5 5 True 5
6 6 False The loop ends

Python checks the condition six times, but the body runs only five times. At the final check, count is 6, so count <= 5 is False and no sixth iteration begins.

The condition is tested before every pass, including the first. If it is False immediately, the body does not run. A while loop therefore runs its body zero or more times.

Indentation determines which statements repeat. Adding a statement after the loop makes the difference visible:

count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1
print("Done")

Both indented statements belong to the loop, so both repeat. print("Done") is dedented, which ends the loop’s block. It runs once, after the condition becomes False.

Chapter 10 used boundary cases to check selection. Loop boundaries require the same care. Here, count <= 3 includes 3; count < 3 would stop before printing it. This difference can cause an off-by-one error, where a loop repeats once too often or once too few.

The flowchart below shows the two possible paths after a condition check:

In the first counting example, the diamond represents count <= 5 and the loop body contains print(count) and count += 1. Following the True path brings execution back to the same condition; the False path leaves the loop.

13.2.1 Avoiding Infinite Loops

If nothing in a loop changes the condition, the loop may never stop:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)

This program repeatedly prints 1. An infinite loop keeps iterating because its condition remains True. Press Ctrl-C in the terminal to interrupt a program stuck in a loop.

An update can be present and still move in the wrong direction:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count -= 1

After the first iteration, count becomes 0, then -1, then -2. All these values are still less than or equal to 5, so the condition never becomes False. The starting value, condition, and update must work together for a counting loop to stop.

A Useful Habit

Before running a counting loop, trace its starting value through two updates and check the condition each time. If the values move away from the stopping point, fix the update first.

13.2.2 Validating Input with while and break

We can now express Chapter 9’s validation flowchart with a while loop. It reads a weight, checks it, and returns to the input step if the weight is invalid.

The break statement ends the nearest loop immediately. In this example, while True keeps the loop running until a positive weight reaches break. Execution then continues with the shipping-rate decision.

As before, assume the input can be converted to a number. The loop checks whether it is positive; handling text that cannot be converted comes later.

The input statement runs at the start of every iteration:

while True:
    weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))
    if weight > 0:
        break
    print("Weight must be positive.")

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

print(f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}")

If the first weight is 1.5, weight > 0 is True, so break leaves the loop before the error message. If the first weight is 0, the program displays the error, then the next iteration reads another weight. For the inputs this program expects, the loop ends with a positive weight for the shipping-rate decision.

Suppose the user enters 0, then -2, then 1.5. Trace the decision after each input:

Value entered weight > 0 What happens next
0 False Display the error and ask again
-2 False Display the error and ask again
1.5 True Run break and leave the loop

The loop ends only when break runs, so the program keeps asking until the user enters a valid weight.

The same pattern applies to other inputs:

  1. Start a while True loop and read a value inside it.
  2. If the value is valid, use break to leave the loop.
  3. Otherwise, explain the problem and let the next iteration ask again.

13.3 The for Statement

The for loop visits the characters of a string one at a time:

course = "COMP"
for letter in course:
    print(letter)

Read the header as “for each letter in course.” Here, letter is the loop variable. On each iteration, Python automatically assigns the next character to it and runs the indented block. When there are no characters left, the loop ends.

Iteration Value of letter Output
1 "C" C
2 "O" O
3 "M" M
4 "P" P

An empty string contains no characters, so a for loop over "" runs zero times. A one-character string produces exactly one iteration.

Three details matter:

  • The loop variable should have a singular name, such as letter, because it refers to one character at a time.
  • The header ends with a colon.
  • The statements in the loop’s block are indented.

A for loop can contain more than one statement:

word = "Code"
for letter in word:
    print(letter)
    print(letter.lower())
print("Done")

Both indented statements run for each character. print("Done") is outside the loop, so it runs once after the final character.

A condition inside the loop can choose how to handle each character:

course = "COMP 1510"

for character in course:
    if character == " ":
        print("space")
    else:
        print(character)

The loop still visits every character, including the space. The if statement chooses which print() call runs during each iteration.

13.4 A Simple Accumulator

An accumulator is a variable initialized before a loop and updated inside it to build a running result. This example counts lowercase "a" characters in a word:

word = "banana"
count = 0

for letter in word:
    if letter == "a":
        count += 1

print(count)

In the earlier while loop, count controlled when repetition stopped. Here, it begins at 0 and increases for each matching letter; its final value is the result.

Each statement has a deliberate position. Initialization belongs before the loop; placing count = 0 inside the loop would erase the earlier work on every iteration. The update belongs inside the if because only a matching character should increase the count. The final print(count) belongs after the loop because the program should report the completed result once.

Trace the value carefully:

letter letter == "a" count after the iteration
"b" False 0
"a" True 1
"n" False 1
"a" True 2
"n" False 2
"a" True 3

The loop checks every letter, while the if statement changes count only for a match.

The comparison matches lowercase "a" only. Convert the input to lowercase first to count uppercase and lowercase forms:

word = input("Word: ")
word = word.lower()
count = 0

for letter in word:
    if letter == "a":
        count += 1

print(f"The word contains the letter a {count} times.")

The counting loop is unchanged; the program now reads and lowercases the word first.

13.5 Tracing Loops by Hand

Chapters 9 and 10 showed how to trace a flowchart or a decision with a chosen input. Apply the same technique to a loop by recording the small set of values that change. For a while loop, record its condition and changing value; if it uses break, record when that statement runs. For a for loop, record the current character and any accumulator.

A useful trace does not need to reproduce every line of the program. It only needs enough information to answer three questions:

  1. What value controls or advances the loop?
  2. What changes during this iteration?
  3. What must eventually cause the loop to stop?

For a while loop, pay particular attention to the first pass and the condition check or break that ends it. For a for loop, follow the first and last items, and consider what happens with an empty string. These cases help reveal incorrect initial values, comparisons, and updates.

13.6 Choosing Between while and for

Use for when you need to work through the items in a sequence. To count the "a" characters in a word, you need to examine every character, so for is a natural choice.

Use while when you need to repeat an action based on a condition or until a decision inside the loop tells you to stop. To get a positive package weight, the program asks on each pass and uses break when the weight is valid. The values the user enters determine how many times the loop repeats.

13.7 Summary

A loop repeats an indented block. A while loop checks its condition before each pass. It stops when the condition becomes False or a break statement ends it. Input validation can use while True to ask again until the value is valid.

A for loop visits a string’s characters one at a time; its loop variable holds each character in turn. An accumulator starts before a loop and builds a running result inside it.
